c-surface-inventory.description: No C tier gate has passed yet, so no generic C item claims source or binary compatibility, whatever part of it the libxmlsec1-compatible library already implements.

c-layer-exclusions.description: The libxmlsec1-compatible headers replace every function the library does not offer by a note naming it and declare none of libxmlsec1's internal crypto-library exports.

backend-tier.description: No backend header is shipped, and every backend-specific entry point is either a provider-limited transform or explicitly unsupported; none is planned or aliased.

native-algorithm-tests.description: The claimed URI set is cross-checked against the native algorithm parsers and the repository's unit and interop suites.

xpath-compatibility-tests.description: XPath and XPath Filter 2.0 use standards behavior by default; integration tests exercise the explicit libxmlsec1-compatible here() binding.

opc-relationship-tests.description: The public pipeline executes case-insensitive SourceType selection and canonical relationship normalization under the default 2021 contract. Dedicated integration tests exercise typed editions, MCE, budgets, and reciprocal 2012 interoperability.

xslt-transform-tests.description: With the xslt feature the public pipeline executes the XSLT transform under the operation's transform policy and XSLT resource limits; without it the URI is reported unsupported. Reciprocal xmlsec1 tests and the donor vectors exercise byte-exact libxslt output.

legacy-policy-tests.description: Legacy SHA-1 and optional historical mechanisms require explicit compatibility policy permission; optional methods also require the legacy-algorithms build feature.

sha1-verification-tests.description: SHA-1 interoperability verification executes through the public pipeline; secure signing defaults reject SHA-1 while an explicit compatibility policy enables builder construction and signing.

provider-contract.description: Only backend transform classes backed by native provider operations are provider-limited; every other backend-specific C entry point is explicitly unsupported.

native-cli-tests.description: Process tests cover native command parsing, exit statuses, sign/verify and encrypt/decrypt paths; the unmodified upstream DSig, Enc, and Keys runners exercise the same binary and capability registry.

phaos-xmldsig-tests.description: The exhaustive Phaos integration suite executes every signature document through the public verification API and asserts exact valid, invalid, or unsupported outcomes without skips.

xmldsig2ed-tests.description: The Second Edition suite executes every signed document and generation template through the public API across compiled XML backends, with exact XSLT outcomes for builds with and without the xslt feature.

planned-surface.description: Unimplemented backend APIs, CLI, registry, format, URI, and donor-suite entries remain machine-readable planned work.

deprecated-surface.description: Deprecated generic functions are declared by the libxmlsec1-compatible headers like the rest of the generic C surface; deprecated backend functions follow the backend classification.

rules.rationale: RSA-PSS fixed URI signing and verification execute through CryptoProvider with exact digest-sized salt and matching MGF1; the complete upstream PSS family is exercised by public pipeline tests.
RSA-PSS SHA-1 is implemented but requires explicit legacy signature policy permission.

The native Rust API implements XPath and XPath Filter 2.0 with standards-compliant here() semantics by default; reproducing libxmlsec1's divergent Transform-element binding requires the explicit XmlSecLegacy mode.
The native Rust API parses and executes this standard URI, with unit or interoperability coverage in the repository.
The complete OPC relationship mechanism uses the 2021 edition by default; the native CLI explicitly selects the 2012 edition required for libxmlsec1 interoperability.
The native Rust API implements SHA-1 reference digests; secure signing defaults reject SHA-1 while an explicit compatibility policy can opt in.
The implementation retains this legacy algorithm for interoperability, but the compiled policy must explicitly permit it.

The legacy-algorithms feature implements this mechanism through RustCrypto. Library defaults deny it; an explicit immutable algorithm allowlist is required. Other providers may report the capability unavailable without fallback.

The optional xslt feature executes XSLT 1.0 stylesheets without external resources and within the operation's XSLT resource limits. Secure profiles exclude it from their transform allowlists; the default and libxmlsec1-compatible policies permit it when built. Stylesheets are read as elements of the signed document by default, with every namespace in scope; the libxmlsec1-compatible profile and the CLI compile the Transform content alone and skip unbound prefix-list entries, as libxmlsec1 and libxslt do.
The URI is part of the libxmlsec1 1.3.13 public vocabulary but is not yet implemented by the native Rust API.

The native provider contract implements the algorithm of this transform, whose URI the native API claims; this backend-specific symbol is not provided, because no backend header is shipped. From C, the generic klass identity of a digest, signature or HMAC algorithm runs it through the provider; the cipher, key-wrap and key-transport klasses report not implemented until the encryption context is provided.

The backend-specific source tier is not claimed for any backend, and no backend header is shipped, so code using this item fails to compile instead of reaching an alias. Entry points that take or return the backend's own objects (EVP_PKEY, X509, BIO, CERTCertificate, gnutls and gcrypt handles, CNG and CryptoAPI handles) cannot exist in a library that consumes no C library; the others have a generic counterpart (xmlSecCrypto*, xmlSecCryptoApp*, xmlSecTransform*Id, xmlSecKeyData*Id) dispatched to the built-in provider.
The libxmlsec1-compatible headers declare this deprecated function with libxmlsec1's behavior, like the rest of the generic C surface, for which no C tier is claimed yet.

The library reads and writes no file and loads no external entity, and has no libxml2 parser context: the libxmlsec1-compatible headers replace this declaration by a note, so a program using it fails to compile, and the caller reads the bytes and passes them to the memory counterpart.

libxmlsec1 exports this function from an uninstalled header for its own crypto libraries, which parse keys and verify certificates outside the core's trust transition; loading one over this library is not supported, and the built-in klasses use crate-private equivalents over the core key readers.

No C tier is claimed yet: the libxmlsec1-compatible headers declare this item as libxmlsec1 does, a declared function the library does not implement yet fails at link time under its own name, and no generic source or binary ABI tier gate has passed.
libxmlsec1 registry entry points are inventoried for the future compatibility layer and are not exposed by the native API.
The native binary implements the libxmlsec1 command spelling and dispatch contract while capability checks delimit the available algorithm and key-data subsets.
The native CLI accepts this donor runner argument, but does not yet implement libxmlsec1's flag-controlled detailed error mode.
The native CLI implements this provider-independent option with donor-compatible parsing and command behavior.

The native CLI maps this libxmlsec1 limit onto the compatibility profile's typed resource policy: the KeyInfo child count, which the core counts before selecting a key and caps at its own ceiling, and the XPath evaluation work, which the core measures itself rather than in libxml2 operations.
Successful operations exit zero and parse, policy, capability, verification, cryptographic, and I/O failures exit non-zero.
This libxmlsec1 option or special status behavior is inventoried but is not yet reproduced by the native CLI.
Native Rust key parsing exists, but the libxmlsec1 key-format enum contract is not yet reproduced.

Every signed vector and generation template is executable and classified by the native public-pipeline suite; its XSLT vectors execute only when the optional xslt feature is built, so family parity is not claimed for the default build.

Every signature vector is executable and classified by the native public-pipeline suite; full family parity remains planned until its explicitly reported HMAC-MD5 and MD5-signed certificate dependencies are implemented. Its XSLT vectors execute when the optional xslt feature is built.
The upstream family is tracked as a parity target; individual covered vectors are recorded by native interoperability tests rather than claiming the whole family.
